unit.event: A specific, dated occurrence involving the security sector or the civil-military balance in a tracked country: an action, decision, incident, deployment, arrest, statement, vote or ruling. One event = one incident; several reports of it are merged into the same record.
unit.analysis: An explainer, op-ed, retrospective, trend piece, podcast or newsletter roundup. Kept and coded for subject, but shown apart from events and never counted in event statistics.
unit.profile: A profile of a person, armed group or criminal organization. Coded like analysis.
unit.relevance: Relevant only if the item has a clear security-sector or civil-military dimension in a tracked Latin American or Caribbean country. Domestic policing is in scope only when it involves militarization, emergency powers, abuse by security forces, or an organized crime–state nexus. Pure crime reporting, weather, sport and general politics without a security dimension are out.

domains.label: Civil–military control
domains.note: The core of the monitor: who commands the coercive apparatus and on what terms.

types.label: Coup or coup plot
types.definition: Concrete, observable and unconstitutional action by members of the ruling regime or of the military or security apparatus to oust the incumbent leader, or to prevent a presumptive leader from taking power (Colpus). A coup succeeds when the leader loses power and the new holders keep it for at least seven days, or the regime changes.
include: Military coup attempts (at least one member of the coercive apparatus acts)
Non-military coup attempts by civilian regime insiders
Plots uncovered by authorities, and officers' public calls to intervene. SENTINEL tracks these as warning signs; Colpus excludes them because no concrete action occurred.
exclude: Trials for past coup attempts → accountability
Analysis of coup risk → content type analysis
types.example: Bolivian army commander leads troops into Plaza Murillo and is arrested hours later.

types.label: Command change or purge
types.definition: Elimination (dismissal, forced retirement, arrest, exile or killing) of individuals with legitimate access to armed force: officers of the military, police or paramilitary forces, and the civilian heads of the security apparatus such as defence and interior ministers (after the MPD dataset).
include: Dismissal of service chiefs or high command
Command reshuffles after a political crisis
exclude: Routine scheduled rotations (code only if salient; salience low)
Removal of civilian ministers without command changes → friction or other
types.example: Colombia's president removes 11 generals in a single week.

types.label: Coup-proofing
types.definition: Deliberate strategies that insulate a ruler from military challenge.
include: Parallel or counterbalancing forces outside the regular chain of command (see the State Security Forces dataset)
Economic co-optation of the officer corps
Surveillance or counter-intelligence aimed at officers
exclude: One-off appointments without a pattern → purge
types.example: (Illustrative) Government creates a presidential guard reporting directly to the executive, outside the army chain of command.

types.label: Military role expansion
types.definition: The armed forces take on, or are formally given, functions normally held by civilian or police authorities.
include: Military assigned to public security, prisons, customs, ports or borders
Military control of civilian administration or state enterprises
exclude: Emergency decrees themselves → emergency_rule (the deployment they authorize is coded here as a secondary type)
Combat operations → conflict
types.example: Congress approves the transfer of the National Guard to the Defence Ministry.
types.note: Subtypes align with the analyst knowledge base's role domains: public security and governance tasks (external defence and political influence are covered by other types).

types.label: Civil–military friction
types.definition: Open disagreement or political signalling between civilian authorities and the armed forces, short of a coup.
include: Officers' public statements on politics or elections
Disputes over budgets, doctrine or command authority
Civilian leaders publicly disciplining or courting the military
Mutinies and defections of units or commanders (definitions follow the MMDD database)
exclude: Removals that follow → purge
types.example: (Illustrative) The army commander publicly questions the election authority days before the vote.

domains.label: Security governance and accountability
domains.note: How the security sector is designed, funded, equipped and held to account.

types.label: Security sector reform
types.definition: Changes to the laws, structure, doctrine, budget or civilian oversight of the security sector.
exclude: Arms purchases → procurement
Trials → accountability
types.example: (Illustrative) Senate passes a law placing military intelligence under civilian oversight.

types.label: Accountability and justice
types.definition: Investigations, prosecutions, rulings or sanctions concerning security personnel or security policy, including transitional justice.
include: Criminal cases against officers or officials
Transitional justice bodies and their rollback
exclude: Arrests of criminals by the forces → oc or conflict
types.example: Colombia's Vice Minister of Defence is sent to trial for procedural fraud.

types.label: Procurement and arms
types.definition: Acquisition, sale or transfer of weapons systems, platforms or defence services.
exclude: Grant-funded equipment from a foreign government → aid
types.example: Argentina signs for 24 F-16 fighters from Denmark.

domains.label: Coercion and rights
domains.note: How the state's coercive power is used against its own population, and how society pushes back.

types.label: State repression
types.definition: Use of state coercion against civilians or political opponents.
include: Internal military deployment against unarmed civilians that kills at least one noncombatant (M3 military repression; flag with subtype military_repression)
exclude: Combat with armed groups → conflict
Protests where forces do not act against civilians → protest
types.example: Rights group reports the 60th death in state custody since April.

types.label: Protest and mobilization
types.definition: Collective action concerning security policy, security forces or the civil-military order, or by security personnel themselves.
include: Protests against militarization, abuses or emergency rule
Police or soldier strikes and protests
exclude: General economic protests with no security dimension (not relevant)
types.example: Unions and prisoners' families march on Miraflores demanding releases and an election date.

domains.label: Armed violence and organized crime
domains.note: Decision rule: armed confrontation involving state forces is conflict; criminal-economy activity and crime–state collusion without combat is organized crime.

types.label: Armed conflict
types.definition: Armed confrontation or offensive operations between state forces and organized armed actors, or major attacks by those actors on the state.
include: Combat with insurgents, dissidents, paramilitaries or armed criminal groups
Attacks on soldiers, police or bases
exclude: Seizures and arrests without combat → oc
State violence against civilians → repression
types.example: Army offensive against Los Pachenca leaves Santa Marta in a fragile calm.

types.label: Organized crime and the state
types.definition: Criminal economies and organizations where they intersect with security forces or the state.
include: Interdictions, seizures and arrests of criminal leaders
Collusion or corruption involving security forces
Negotiations, tacit pacts or truces between state actors and criminal groups
exclude: Armed clashes → conflict
Crime stories with no state or security dimension (not relevant)
types.example: Shield of the Americas blacklists 24 criminal groups.

types.label: Peace process
types.definition: Negotiation, ceasefire, disarmament or demobilization with armed groups.
exclude: Combat after a breakdown → conflict
types.example: The Conquistadores de la Sierra announce the end of their armed strike.

domains.label: External security relations
domains.note: Foreign governments and militaries acting on the region's security sector.

types.label: Security cooperation and foreign operations
types.definition: Foreign military or security presence, joint operations and exercises, intelligence sharing, agreements, or direct foreign military action.
include: Bilateral or multinational exercises, drills and naval port visits
Intelligence sharing between governments or security services (agreements, joint centres, targeting support)
Foreign sanctions or designations aimed at a country's security sector
exclude: Foreign-funded intelligence training or equipment → aid
Funding and equipment grants → aid
Boundary inside the type: planned drills and visits are exercise_* or port_visit; real operations are joint_operation or direct_foreign_operation
types.example: US removes Venezuela from its drug-trafficking blacklist (external_pressure).

types.label: Security assistance
types.definition: Foreign funding, training or equipment for security forces.
include: FMF, IMET, INCLE and similar programmes
Intelligence training or equipment provided by a foreign government
exclude: Purchases → procurement
types.example: Washington approves $461M in security assistance for Colombia.

domains.label: Political context with a security dimension
domains.note: Political decisions and contests where the security dimension is explicit: exceptional powers and elections.

types.label: Emergency rule
types.definition: Declarations, extensions or uses of exceptional powers that expand the role or authority of security forces.
include: States of exception, siege or emergency
Leaders explicitly using an emergency to justify an expanded security role
exclude: Purely humanitarian disaster declarations with no security role
types.example: Ecuador's president decrees a state of exception in eight provinces citing grave internal commotion.

types.label: Elections and security
types.definition: Elections where security forces, political violence or a security agenda are central.
exclude: Routine election news (not relevant)
types.example: Crime dominates Brazil's campaign ahead of the 4 October first round.

types.label: Other
types.definition: Relevant but not captured above. Requires a one-line reason in coding_note. Target: under 5% of events.

migration: Repression of protests moves to repression
Custodial deaths and detentions move to repression; seizures to oc
friction, accountability, electoral_security, military_role or other
Recoded; the remainder needs a reason
decisions: Decided 29 Sep: exercise is a subtype of cooperation; procurement stays its own type (arms-flow and defence-industry analysis). 18 types.
Decided 29 Sep: keep DEED and axis, required on every event, coded independently of type (see Fields).
Decided 29 Sep: Colpus definition for coup and MPD definition for purge.
Decided 29 Sep: use only the 35 DEED categories most relevant to the monitor, to supplement the political dimension.
Decided 29 Sep: salience target of about 10–15% high.
Decided 29 Sep: domestic policing is in scope only with militarization, emergency powers, abuse by security forces, or an organized crime–state nexus.
Decided 29 Sep: every v3 record keeps its v2 family as legacy_event_family, so historical charts and the risk models keep working during the switch.

Deferred 29 Sep: evidence tiers (documented, credible, alleged) from the analyst knowledge base are not part of v3. Reconsider for a later version, for example to require documented or credible evidence before coding collusion or corruption. Corroboration, computed from source count and tier, covers source strength for now.

actors.intro: Built on the existing actor taxonomy (config/taxonomy/actor_types.json): category → group → type, with roles. Today the classifier ignores it and picks from 7 flat codes; all 2,303 actor codings come from keyword rules, 87% at low confidence, and the 399-entry registry is mostly one generic placeholder per group per country. v3 has the classifier extract named actors and link them to the registry.
groups: Armed forces and their branches, defence ministry
National and local police, gendarmeries, national guards under civilian command
Ministerio del Poder Popular para el Servicio Penitenciario
Foreign armed forces and commands (new; split from foreign_government)
Guerrillas and dissident factions with political aims (new; split from armed_non_state_actor)
Colectivos, Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada
Cartels, gangs and trafficking networks (new; split from armed_non_state_actor)
CJNG, Tren de Aragua, Los Pachenca
Foro Penal, Un Mundo Sin Mordaza
Protesters and the civilian population as a collective
rules: Name actors as the source does, then link them to the registry by name and alias; unmatched names go to a registry review queue instead of becoming generic placeholders.
Each actor gets one role. Every event needs at least one initiator unless the source names none.
Use the most specific unit named (the DGCIM, not 'the military'), with its parent kept in the registry so counts roll up.
A foreign government acting through its armed forces is foreign_military; through diplomacy, sanctions or aid it is foreign_government.
actors.registry_growth: Seed the registry with the named actors the monitor already tracks (FANB components, DGCIM, SEBIN, Guardia Nacional, ELN, EMC, Clan del Golfo, Los Pachenca, CJNG, Sinaloa factions, Tren de Aragua, MS-13, Barrio 18, colectivos) before classification, so the first run links rather than invents.

deed.intro: SENTINEL codes each event's role in democratic erosion with the Democratic Erosion Event Dataset (DEED) and Autocratic Consolidation Event (ACE) codebook, v7 (Fall 2025). DEED supplements the political dimension: type says what happened, DEED says what it does to accountability. SENTINEL uses 35 of DEED's 84 categories, the ones that concern the security sector, civil–military relations and security-linked political change; categories about party systems, media markets, minorities, education and the economy are left out.
types: A warning sign that can lead to erosion before any institutional change.
Citizens or institutions pushing back against erosion.
An event that undermines the stability of an autocratic regime.
No bearing on democratic accountability. Must be chosen explicitly.

categories.3.2.12: Rhetorical Attacks against Democracy or Accountability Institutions
categories.4.1.4: Suspension of Laws or the Constitution
categories.6.2.1: Transfer of Power from Authoritarian Leaders
categories.6.3.3: State Attempts at Democratization or to Prevent Backsliding

rules: DEED type is coded on every event (not_applicable allowed). DEED category is added when one of the listed categories fits; otherwise it stays empty.
The category must sit under the chosen DEED type.
Axis is derived from the category's group (horizontal, vertical); when no category applies, axis is coded directly.
DEED never decides the event type, and the event type never decides DEED.

foundations: DEED types and all 84 categories; axis; actor levels (central, state/local, civil society, external).
Colpus coup dataset codebook (Chin, Wright and Carter 2021)
Coup definition, military vs non-military attempts, the success rules.
Purge definition and who counts as a purge target.
Parallel and counterbalancing forces for coup-proofing.
Mutiny and defection subtypes under friction.
Multidimensional Measures of Militarization, M3 (Bayer et al. 2023)
Military repression, veto power and impunity; crosswalk to militarization indicators.
Crosswalk for the structural indicators on country pages.
Coup-proofing and civilian control literature (Jin; Kenwick; Sudduth; Böhmelt et al.; Albrecht)
Concept definitions and the private latent-variable work.
Military role domains, civil–military relationship types, crime–state interaction types.
Country notes on what each military does.
crosswalk: Colpus; M3 military leader and regime origin
6.3.3 State Attempts at Democratization…; 4.1.x when reforms concentrate power
4.2.1 Repression of the Opposition; 4.2.4 Curtailed Civil Liberties; 4.2.5 Media Repression; 3.2.6 State-Conducted Violence or Abuse

4.1.4 Suspension of Laws or the Constitution

fields.name: type / subtype
fields.values: one type from the domains above; one subtype from its list or null
fields.rule: Pick the most specific type. Precedence when two fit: coup > emergency_rule > repression > conflict > oc > military_role > others.

fields.name: secondary_types
fields.rule: For events that clearly belong to more than one category (for example, an emergency decree that deploys the army: emergency_rule + military_role).

fields.name: country / secondary_countries
fields.values: one tracked country (or Regional); list of others
fields.rule: Primary = where the event happens. Replaces pipe-joined values like Colombia|Venezuela.

fields.name: event_date / date_precision
fields.values: YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or null; day | month | unknown
fields.rule: When the event happened, taken from the text. Publication date is stored separately and never substituted.

fields.name: location
fields.values: place, state or department, precision (place | admin1 | country)
fields.rule: Most specific place named. Geocoded against a gazetteer; unresolved places keep country precision.

fields.name: actors[]
fields.values: up to 4 named actors, each with name, group, role and country
fields.rule: See section 4. Each actor also gets a level: central, subnational, civil society or external (DEED).

fields.name: salience
fields.rule: High: could shift the country's civil-military status or outlook (coup, top-command purge, new or extended emergency rule, state violence with 10+ victims, direct foreign military action, landmark reform or ruling). Medium: notable national development in a tracked category. Low: routine, local or background. Target about 10–15% high.

fields.name: certainty
fields.rule: The coder's certainty that the coding is right, given the text. Separate from corroboration, which is computed from the number and tier of sources and never asked of the model.

fields.name: deed_type
fields.rule: Coded on every event; see section 5. Independent of type.

fields.name: deed_category
fields.values: one of the 35 DEED v7 categories in section 5.2, or empty
fields.rule: Added when a listed category fits; must sit under the chosen DEED type.

fields.name: axis
fields.rule: Derived from the DEED category's group when there is one; coded directly otherwise.

fields.name: summary
fields.values: English, one sentence, at most 40 words
fields.rule: Neutral, no publisher names, translate if needed.

fields.name: evidence
fields.values: 1–2 short quotes from the source text
fields.rule: The phrases that support the type and the date. Shown to analysts; lets any code be checked in seconds.

fields.name: episode_id
fields.rule: Links reports of one unfolding sequence (the feed's story rows), following the process–episode–event schema. Assigned after coding, not by the classifier.

fields.name: relationship_signal
fields.values: subordinate | bargaining | tutelary_veto | partisan_pillar | fractured | praetorian | corruption_capture | null
fields.rule: Optional, high-salience events only: what the event shows about the civil–military relationship (analyst knowledge base). Kept separate from the military's role.
